**Verdict:** Hormozi wouldn't give you a "good" churn percentage. He'd tell you to find the number one reason people cancel and fix it, and his own example says that reason is usually overwhelm, not a lack of value. The vault has no benchmark figure or alarm threshold from him, only how he cut churn in his own paid community.

**Based on:** he said this about cancellations in his own paid community, Skool Games. The benchmark part of your question is beyond the vault.

**Why he'd say it**
- He diagnosed churn by the reason people left: "basically the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm. It was not oh I need to provide more value. It was I need to provide more value per second in fewer total seconds." ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s) to 11:35)
- He describes how members drop off: "Oh my god, there's so many things I have to do. I can't think about it." And then they leave ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)).
- His rule for fixing it is to take things away: "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value" (@ 11:35). He also asks "how much can I take away and still have it be good and not only be good but it probably is better" (@ 11:02).
- Applied to your question, it follows from what he said: worry when people leave because the community is too much work to keep up with, not just when the percentage looks high. Ask the people who cancel why they left. If the answer is "too much," adding more content will make churn worse.

**What he's done:** In Skool Games he cut the weekly calls from three to one and moved the big content release from monthly to quarterly. He also switched off app features so new members had fewer things to do when they joined ([@ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)).

**Beyond the vault (not in the vault):** He often frames churn as a ceiling on how big a business can get. Your member count levels off at new members per month divided by monthly churn. So 100 new members a month at 10% churn caps you around 1,000 members, and at 5% churn around 2,000. Churn tells you when growth will stop, not whether a number is "good." I'm confident he teaches this idea, but it isn't quoted in this vault. I also can't find a specific "good churn %" for communities that I'd confidently attribute to him.

**What would change his answer:** nothing in the sources. This vault covers only six sources, and none of them is about retention metrics.

My own view, separate from his: low-priced paid communities often lose somewhere around 5–15% of members a month, and most of those losses come in the first 30–60 days. So track churn by how long people have been members, not only as one overall rate.

**Verdict:** Take the percentage of revenue. Hormozi's position is to take top line, not profit, because the owner controls the expenses, and "profit" can be cut to nothing before you're paid. Your share should depend on a number you can see and the owner can't easily shrink.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault. The `hormozi-pre` vault has nothing where he talks about profit-share versus revenue-share deals. I ran several searches (profit, revenue, percent, equity, partner, consulting) over both the wiki and the raw transcripts. The core answer comes from what I know of his public teaching, and I've labelled it.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Profit is a number the owner controls (not in the vault).** He has repeatedly told people to take a share of revenue over a share of profit. The owner decides salaries, perks, reinvestment and when to expand, and every one of those choices moves "profit." A profit share ties your pay to decisions you don't make. It also makes every expense line a potential fight.
- **Revenue is the part your work moves.** If your consulting grows sales, a revenue share pays you for that directly. A profit share can pay you nothing for the same result if the client spends it.
- **His own deals are equity, not profit splits (in the vault).** At Acquisition.com he "usually" buys "minority Stakes 25 to 49 is percent" and acts as "growth Partners um we come in we write a check we add value we help grow the business" ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1972s) @ 32:52 to 33:58). When he's paid for helping a company grow, he owns a stake. He doesn't wait on someone else's bottom line.

**What would change his answer (not in the vault):**
- **Revenue share can be bad for the client.** If the client's margins are thin, a revenue share could make your deal unprofitable for them. A deal that hurts the client tends to get cut, so in that case he'd want a smaller percentage of revenue rather than a switch to profit.
- **A profit share needs protection.** If you do take profit, insist on clear definitions and audit rights: what counts as an expense, and a cap on the owner's pay.
- **With real leverage, he'd push for more.** He'd ask for equity, or a fee plus a percentage. That's the Acquisition.com model, where you're paid even if growth is slow.

If you want to keep this answer, I can save it to `derived/` in the vault, labelled as outside the vault.

**Verdict: Bootstrap.** For a first business, Hormozi would tell you to have customers fund it, not investors. Sell something expensive to a few people, live on that income, and put every other dollar back into growth.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has no clip where he weighs "investors vs. bootstrap" head-on, but his stated playbook for starting from zero is all customer-funded.

**Why he'd say it**
- **His named "bootstrap strategy."** Asked how he'd start over in 2026, he says to sell your own time one-on-one at a premium: "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)). It "can allow you to live on this and then cash flow all the growth" (same timestamp). He also says "If you trade your time for the money, you have a 100% margin" ([@ 6:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=360s)).
- **It doesn't need to scale yet.** "it doesn't have to be scalable" ([@ 2:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=129s)). He also calls it "a great way to beta test ideas" ([@ 4:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=297s)). So his answer to "I need capital to build the scalable version" is: you don't need that version yet.
- **Growth money comes from the money model, not a cap table.** His focus is how to "pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion uh within a business so that you can scale" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). The goal is "to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" (same timestamp). If customers cost too much to get: "do what you can control, make more from each one" ([@ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)).

**What he's done**
- At his early gym, one cash-paying personal-training client covered his living costs, so all the gym's money went into growth ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)).
- In 2016 he was down to $1,000. He got out by selling: about $300,000 in a month that was "basically all profit," which covered $150K in refunds ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 30:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1802s)). Gym Launch then did $26M top line in its first 12 months. The vault shows no investor money in that story.

**Not in the vault, but widely known about him:** he often says he never raised outside money for his companies. His firm, Acquisition.com, invests in businesses that are already working, not in first-time founders' ideas.

**What would change his answer:** the vault doesn't say. My guess, not his words: a business that can't make money before a big upfront build, like hardware or deep tech, falls outside this playbook.

**Caveat:** that 2025 video opens its description with a link to his own scaling-roadmap lead magnet, so the advice also feeds his funnel. The funding logic stands on its own anyway.

My own view: for a first business, I agree with him.

**Verdict:** Hormozi wouldn't hand you a daily schedule. He'd tell you to pick the one input that gets you more customers, do far more of it every day than feels reasonable, and say no to everything else. If you're young and have no dependants, he'd also tell you to work as many hours as you can.

His reasoning: a business that makes some money but not enough has one constraint holding it back. Your hours should go to that constraint, not to admin, tweaking things or new ideas.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault never covers how he lays out a day. These are his principles on focus, volume and hours, applied to your situation.

**Why he'd say it**

- **Your workday is one problem, not a to-do list.** His test is "what one thing if it were true 12 months from now would change everything for our business" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 3:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=232s)). As a solo owner you are the CEO, so naming it is your job. He's blunt about the rest: "sometimes you have to let the little fires burn" ([@ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).
- **"Not enough money" usually means more customers, or making each one worth more.** He defines growth that way: "well get more customers make them worth more" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 35:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2137s)). Each day should push one of those two numbers. When gym owners told him they just needed more leads, he took that as the one thing that mattered.
- **Put the hours into inputs you can count.** "if you do not know the inputs that are going to get the output that you want then what are you doing" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 38:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2304s)). On sales, his rule is volume: "do twice the volume" of the best rep, so the stretch where you're bad is shorter in calendar days ([@ 40:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2402s)). At his first gym he taught every class and still ran sales consults at 8, 9, 10 and 11 p.m. for about six months ([@ 55:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=3305s)).
- **Volume beats cleverness.** "you just have to do so much volume that it is unreasonable that you fail" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 9:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=544s)). Reading and watching videos don't count as work: "you entertained yourself. You did not educate yourself" ([@ 5:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=339s)).
- **Hours depend on your situation.** "if you're under 30 and you have no responsibilities, I recommend working as many hours per week as humanly possible" ([@ 11:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=712s)). He softens it for people with kids, who have trade-offs but more experience to spend effort strategically. For himself, he works until his output per hour drops sharply, then rests.
- **Short on cash? Sell a slice of your time at a premium.** "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)). Use it to fund the business, and cap it.
- **Don't spread your days across new ideas.** "the effort that it takes to compound is the length of time you have to say no to everything else" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s)).

**A day built on those principles** (my synthesis, not his words):
1. Spend the first and largest block of the day on your one constraint, usually getting customers: outreach, content, ads or sales calls. Set a daily number and hit it.
2. If cash is tight, add one capped block of premium one-on-one work.
3. Fit delivery and admin into whatever time is left. Leave anything that doesn't move customers or what each one is worth, and let it burn.
4. Keep going until your output per hour falls off, then rest.

**Not in the vault:** his book *$100M Leads* has a "Rule of 100": 100 primary advertising actions a day (such as outreach or content) for 100 days. That's the closest thing he has to a prescribed workday. This comes from what I know about him, and the vault doesn't quote it.

**What would change his answer:** if you love your life as it is, he says "you've already won", and the max-hours advice doesn't apply. If you have kids or other responsibilities, he'd want effort spent more strategically rather than just more of it.

One caveat: his views on work hours are personal philosophy. His 2023 interview refused to tell anyone how much they "should" work, so the 2025 "work max hours" advice is a newer, conditional stance.

**Verdict:** Keep the cash and put it into growth, as long as the growth spend pays for itself. Paying off debt early isn't something Hormozi treats as a priority. What he cares about is pointing every dollar at customer acquisition that breaks even or better, and making each customer worth more. The exception: if the debt is a "hole" that stops you thinking past this month's bills, clear that first.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from him on paying down business debt specifically. When he says "debt" in these sources he means ignorance ("the biggest debt all of us pay is ignorance"), not loans. This answer applies his cash and growth principles to your situation.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Spend aggressively while you stay at break-even.** On his 2025 book launch: "the goal is to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). For him, cash in a profitable business is fuel for acquisition. Parking it in a paid-down balance takes it out of the engine.
- **Cash speed is the growth lever.** His money-model idea is "how do you pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion uh within a business so that you can scale" ([@ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). If acquisition feels too expensive, his fix is to "make more from each one" ([@ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)), not to pull back.
- **Fund the base, then go aggressive.** He'd rather you raise income than cut exposure: "be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)). For a service business, that could mean a capped premium tier, sold one-on-one, that covers the debt payments.
- **The exception is when you're underwater.** "I get that you can't have a vision if you have bills to pay, if rent is due… this is why I'm such an advocate of like get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 17:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s)). He says this about people struggling to get by, not about profitable owners. Still, it's his rule: if the debt is what keeps you from thinking long-term, deal with it first.

**What he's done:** At his first gym, one cash-paying personal-training client covered his own needs, "so he could reinvest all of the gym's money into growth" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)). He kept the business's cash in growth and funded his living costs from somewhere else.

**What would change his answer:**
- You have no growth channel that reliably pays back at break-even or better. Then there's nothing to "go aggressive" with.
- The debt payments threaten survival or take over your thinking. That's his "get your head above water first" case.

**My own note (not from him):** The interest rate decides this more than his principles do. If the $60k is high-rate debt, like credit cards at 20% or more, paying it off is a guaranteed return that few growth bets beat once you account for risk. If it's cheap term debt, his answer holds.

**Verdict:** Hormozi wouldn't give you a refresh schedule. He'd tell you to keep running a winning hook for as long as it wins ("use it to death") and to spend your effort writing new hooks that try to beat it. You replace an ad when a challenger beats it or its numbers drop, not because a certain number of days has passed.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from him on "ad fatigue" or a refresh interval. He does talk about how to treat winning hooks, and that answers the question.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Ride a winner and keep testing against it.** "if you have a winning hook for your ad campaigns you keep using it to death and you try and beat it" ([14 Years of Marketing Advice in 35 Minutes @ 1:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=73s)). The thing that sets the timing is a challenger beating your current best ad.
- **The hook is where testing pays most.** Going from 1% to 3% click-through triples everyone who sees the rest of your funnel. Elsewhere a "monster split test" gets a 20–50% lift, but "a banger or killer headline can absolutely outperform the control by two three sometimes 5x" ([@ 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=36s)). So he'd put your new work into hooks and headlines, not into rewriting body copy on a schedule.
- **Find new hooks by copying ones that already work.** "look at your organic content or other people's organic content or other people's ads look at the first 3 seconds visually and verbally… can I steal like an artist from a different industry" ([@ 1:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=111s)).
- **The principle underneath is volume.** His 2025 talks keep coming back to doing so many reps that failing becomes unreasonable. For ads, that means a steady stream of new hook tests rather than a quarterly creative overhaul.

**What he's done:** In the vlog of his *$100M Money Models* launch (2025), his team films about 40 ads. Someone on the team says they "grabbed basically every hook that's been working for the existing winners, plus a bunch of the organic ones that did well". They wait for more data to get statistical significance before making new ads. Then someone, probably Hormozi though several people talk in that video, says they'll "take the best hooks that… will still work" ([My final update @ 0:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=33s), [@ 7:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=465s)). New ads were based on the hooks that had already won, and the data decided when.

**What would change his answer:** Nothing in the vault. Going beyond the vault (this is my addition, not something he said): at very high spend, or with a small audience, a winning ad does wear out sooner. That makes the "keep testing to beat the winner" loop more important, but it doesn't make a calendar the trigger.

**My caveat:** In practice, a weekly batch of new hook tests is a good rhythm to run his approach on. That cadence is my suggestion, not his.

**Verdict:** No. He'd tell you to raise prices. An 82% close rate means you're leaving money on the table, and protecting it is the wrong goal. Raise the price on your main job, add a premium tier at about 10x, and stop raising once demand falls off.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has no Hormozi quote about close rates as a pricing signal. His pricing principles cover your case, though.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Your goal should be profit, not close rate.** He calls close rate an incremental lever: "We're not thinking increments. We're thinking orders of magnitude. So yes, if you improve your sales close rate…" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 9:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=595s)). An 82% close rate shows that demand is bigger than your price. His rule for that situation: "when you have demand, cut supply" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 5:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=328s)). A higher price is how you cut supply.
- **Losing a few closes still pays.** Here's my own arithmetic on your numbers, not his. Say you raise prices 20% and your close rate drops from 82% to 70%. If your costs scale with each job, profit per 100 inspections goes up about 30%. You'd only make less money if your close rate fell below roughly 54% (all costs per-job) to 68% (all costs fixed). Most price increases don't cause anywhere near that drop.
- **Add a 10x tier.** "Every business should list an offer 10x above its main one" is the wiki's summary of his advice, not a quote. His own words: "If they want to pay you more money, you should give them the opportunity to do so" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 7:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=425s)). Even at small volume, "lots of zeros still add up" (@ 9:47). The expensive tier also "literally increases the perceived value" of your standard job (@ 7:36).
- **What a premium duct job might include.** Speed and less hassle for the customer: "take whatever the delivery time you currently have is and cut it in half" and "You will always have priority" (@ 16:25). He also says to design it for "a different person," a richer buyer (@ 13:04). For you that could mean next-day service, a whole-home air-quality package, and annual service where they never have to call you.
- **Don't hide the new price or apologize for it.** "You must confront the high price," then "We shut up. We let them talk" (@ 8:09, @ 8:41). If someone says no, offer a cut-down version.
- **Find your best customers.** At a PR firm he invested in, he noticed that 15% of clients bought the top package. He rebuilt the business around only that group and charged 10x, and response rates went up ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:23:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4991s)). Check whether certain homes or zip codes always buy your biggest package.

**Not in the vault:** In his books and other talks (not in this vault), he usually treats a very high close rate as a sign you're underpriced and tells owners to raise prices until it comes down. I can't quote that from here.

**What would change his answer:** In this vault, he only names one case where he'd stay put. He sees two equally good paths: keep raising prices and become the "Versace" with fewer units, or stay cheaper and go for volume ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:29:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5386s)). If you deliberately chose volume and price is what brings in your leads, holding prices fits that choice. Holding them just to protect a close-rate number does not. He also warns that "the middle is where people die" (@ 0:00), and a profitable mid-priced service business is that middle.

My one caveat: test the increase on part of your inspections first, such as one crew, one territory or new leads only. Duct cleaning has cheap "$99 whole-house" competitors, and your close rate may depend on how much people trust you in the home rather than on price.

**Verdict:** Don't start ads yet, but do go after more replacements. Hormozi would have you double down on door knocking, which already works, and turn the doors you already knock into more replacement jobs. Ads come later, once you know what a customer is worth and can buy them at break-even or better.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. Nothing in the vault covers roofing or when to switch from door knocking to ads, so this applies his principles to your numbers. Points marked *(not in the vault)* come from what I know of his other work.

**Why he'd say it**

- **More doors before a new channel.** You're two months in and door knocking is getting results. He tells beginners to do "high volume transactional sales so whether that's you doing door to door or you cold calling" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 39:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2370s)) and to "do twice the volume" ([@ 40:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2402s)). At one sale per 20 doors, revenue is mostly a question of how many doors you knock. In *$100M Leads* he says to do more of what's already working before adding a new lead channel *(not in the vault)*.
- **One thing, not two.** He'd warn against starting a second lead source while the first one isn't maxed out: "me trying to solve it in two or three ways ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)). He also says people underestimate the effort it takes "to stick with one thing rather than jumping to the next shiny opportunity every six months" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1344s)).
- **Replacements, yes, but through your money model rather than ads.** One replacement is worth about 12 to 16 repairs. His rule is to "do what you can control, make more from each one" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)), and a good money model means "offering the right thing at the right time in the right way to the right customer" ([@ 3:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=235s)). For you that means treating every $1,500 repair as a way into a full-roof inspection and a replacement quote. Don't treat repairs as the end of the sale.
- **Knock on better doors.** "Find the people who value what you have the most" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:38:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5918s)). For roofing, that probably means neighborhoods with older roofs, recent storm damage, or higher home values. That's my application of his principle; he didn't say it about roofing. The 20 doors cost you the same either way, and these ones are more likely to need a full replacement.
- **If doors say no, fix the offer before buying traffic.** "If we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:24:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5089s)). Ads put more people in front of the same pitch. If the pitch isn't converting, ads won't fix it.
- **When ads do make sense.** His test for ad spend is "spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). You can only check that once you know your cost per lead, close rate and average job value, including how often a repair later becomes a replacement. Door knocking gives you those numbers for free.

**What he's done:** He learned Facebook ads before opening his first gym ([@ 1:17:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4668s)). So he isn't against ads. He's against buying leads before the offer and the money model are proven.

**What would change his answer:** If you're already knocking every door you physically can and close the replacement leads you get, your own time is the bottleneck. Then he'd say add ads or hire a second door knocker. He'd still use the break-even test, and he'd pick whichever adds volume fastest.

One line of my own: storm areas and insurance claims shape roofing demand much more than gym demand, so which neighborhoods you target probably matters even more than his principle suggests.

I found what I need in the vault. One caution before the answer: it has nothing on affiliates, podcasts or ad-spend walls specifically. So the answer below applies principles he did state to your situation.

**Verdict:** Don't move budget into affiliates and podcasts yet. Fix your money model first, meaning get more money from each customer and get it sooner. That lets you afford a higher cost per customer and keep scaling Meta past $100k. When you do add a channel, add one, not several.

**Based on:** follows from what he said

**Why he'd say it**
- **He sees the wall as an economics problem, not a channel problem.** He describes every business as the gap between the cost of getting a customer and what you make from that customer: "all businesses have the cost of getting customers and what you make from those customers as the core economic arbitrage that makes a business a business" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=0s)). At $100k a month, Meta isn't saturated so much as your per-customer cost has outgrown what each customer pays you.
- **His fix is to make more from each customer, not to find cheaper ones.** "rather than thinking, "Oh, I'm spending too much to get customers, do what you can control, make more from each one."" ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s)). And more bluntly: "Your business isn't growing because you don't have a good enough money model." ([@ 9:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=561s)). Both lines are ad scripts for his own book launch, so they double as sales copy.
- **The goal is maximum spend at break-even or better.** On his 2025 launch: "the goal is to spend as much money as humanly possible uh while maintaining break even or better" ([@ 8:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s)). **What he's done:** His previous book launch had "no offer to liquidate ad spend", so he paid for the ads himself. For the 2025 launch he built a money model first, specifically so he could scale spend at break-even ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 7:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=465s)).

**What would change his answer** (not in the vault, from his book *$100M Leads*): he does list affiliates among the four main ways to get leads, alongside paid ads. His rule there is to max out one channel before adding the next. If your numbers already return the full ad cost quickly, ads are profitable at higher spend, and the wall is creative fatigue, he'd say produce far more ads first. My own note: depending on one ad platform for 85% of customers is a real account-ban risk. The vault doesn't address that, and it may be a reason to start one second channel earlier than he'd suggest.

**Verdict:** No, he'd say do the opposite. Your members are cancelling because the membership is too much work, and more trainings and more calls make it more work. Cut it down to the one thing that gets members their result, and add the next piece only when they need it.

**Based on:** he said it. He ran into this same cancel reason in his own membership and fixed it by removing things.

**Why he'd say it**

- **He faced your exact problem in Skool Games.** He said overwhelm was the top reason people cancelled, and that the answer wasn't more value:
  > "the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm. It was not oh I need to provide more value. It was I need to provide more value per second in fewer total seconds." ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s))

  What he did: he went from three calls a week to one, moved the big content drop from monthly to quarterly, and turned off app features so new members had fewer things to do (@ 11:35). Your plan goes the other direction.
- **Only add something when the member needs it.** "you only introduce something when it's required or necessary for that person to get the the desired value" (@ 11:35). Find "this one thing that most people find valuable first and then perfect that step" (@ 12:08).
- **Start by taking things away.** "how much can I take away and still have it be good and not only be good but it probably is better" (@ 11:02). He also says "complexity is typically the child of lazy thinking. We can't prioritize." (@ 1:43). Piling on bonuses avoids deciding what actually matters.
- **"Can't keep up" is a value problem, not just a usability one.** In his value equation, effort sits underneath the value: "effort are the things that you have to start doing that you don't want to do as a result of this purchase" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:21:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4864s)). Every extra training adds effort and lowers the value a member feels they're getting.
- **"Too expensive" is probably the same problem.** This part is my inference, not something he said. If a member can't use what they pay for, $99 feels like a lot. His idea of value is a result that's likely, fast and easy. A membership that leaves people behind on content fails on all three, however much content it has.

**What he'd have you do** (his principles applied to your case):
1. Pick the one result members join for. Cut everything that isn't the shortest path to it.
2. Hold fewer calls, release content less often, and give new members one first step instead of a library.
3. Cut how long it takes to get a first result. He calls speed his biggest persuasion lever: "latency beats magnitude 7 days a week" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 15:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=953s)).

**What would change his answer:** the vault doesn't give a case where he'd add more. By his own logic, extra material would make sense only if members cancelled because they ran out of things to do. Your cancel reasons point the other way.

**Caveats**
- The Skool story is his own account, in a video that also funnels viewers to Acquisition.com. He gave no before-and-after churn numbers.
- The vault doesn't cover churn benchmarks or keeping members through a better first week. I'd check whether the people who cancel ever finished their first step.
